# Topic 2: Intro to Bash

---

<ul>
	<li>
        Most people communicate with their computer through graphical user
        interfaces (GUI)
    </li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">
        These GUIs are translators
        <ul>
            <li>
                Translates your clicks into instructions
            </li>
        </ul>
    </li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">
        Works well for simple tasks, but does not scale well
        <ul>
            <li>
                E.g., what if you need to gather info from 1000
                files?
            </li>
            <li>
                Click, click, click &#8230;
            </li>
        </ul>
    </li>
</ul>

---

<ul>
	<li>
        If you vacation in a foreign country, a translator is very helpful
    </li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">
        But, what if you move to that country for a job in which you interact
        with hundreds of people every day?
    </li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">
        A translator only gets you so far
    </li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">
        We want to learn the language used by the GUI to talk (more) directly
        to our computer
    </li>
</ul>

## About these slides

I will use a "Bash command line" heading for lines we type at the command prompt

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
echo "Hello World!"
```

I will use a "Bash script" heading for lines we type in a file

```{.bash filename="Bash script"}
echo "Hello World!"
```


# Anatomy of a command

---

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
echo -e "Hello, World!"
```

::: {.incremental}
`echo`
:   Command (program)

`-e`
:   Option or "flag"

`"Hello, World!"`
:   Argument
:::


---

Precision (spelling, case, and spaces) matters

```{.bash filename="Bash command line" code-line-numbers="1|2|3"}
echo - e "hello"
Echo "hello"
eco "hello"
```

## Getting help with a command


```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
man echo
```

<ul>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">
        This shows the manual for the <code class="ilcode">echo</code> command
    </li>
    <ul>
    	<li class="fragment fade-up">
            Navigate with arrow keys (or 'j'/'k')
        </li>
    	<li class="fragment fade-up">
            Press 'q' to exit the manual
        </li>
    </ul>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">
        Note, <code>man</code> is the command (program)
        and <code>echo</code> is an argument
    </li>
</ul>


# File System & Paths

---

::: {.column-body style="text-align: center;"}
<figure>
    <img src="../images/file-system-tree.gif" alt="File-system tree" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto;">
    <figcaption><a href="https://flylib.com/books/en/1.295.1.47/1/">flylib.com</a></figcaption>
</figure>
:::

---

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
pwd
ls /
ls /arc
ls /arc/homes/jro0014
ls
```

`pwd` shows the path to your current location in the file system (***p***rint ***w***orking ***d***irectory)

`ls` lists files and directories

---

Let's make 2 new directories move into/out of them

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
mkdir foo bar
cd foo
pwd
cd ..
pwd
cd /arc/homes/jro0014/foo
pwd
cd ..
```
. . .

<br>

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
cd foo
pwd
cd ../bar # same as cd /arc/homes/jro0014/bar
```

---

How to get home?

-   There are several ways

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
cd
pwd
cd ~
pwd
cd $HOME
pwd
```

---

`$HOME` and `~` are just variables for your home directory

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
echo $HOME
echo ~
```

. . .

You can use these variables for relative paths

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
cd foo
cd ~/bar # same as ../bar or /arc/homes/jro0014/bar
```


# What *are* commands?

---

-   They are just programs!
    -   Files on your computer that can be executed


---

`whereis` is a command for finding files in your `PATH`

```{.bash filename="Bash command line" code-line-numbers="1-3|4-6|7"}
whereis -b pwd
pwd
/bin/pwd
whereis -b ls
ls
/bin/ls
whereis -b whereis
```

---

-   The reason you don't have to type `/bin/pwd` is because `/bin` is in your `PATH`

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
echo $PATH
```

-   When you type `pwd`, Bash will look for it in these directories


# For loop

---

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
for x in 1 2 3 4; do echo hello; done
```

. . .

<br>

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
for x in 1 2 3 4; do echo $x; done
```

---

Let's make a file with one word in it

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
echo how > file1.txt
```

-   "`>`" ***redirects*** the output of `echo` into the file "file1.txt"

. . .

Confirm the `file1.txt` exists and has "how" in it

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
ls
cat file1.txt
```

---

Let's make 2 more files

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
echo are > file2.txt
echo you? > file3.txt
```

---

Let's loop over the files and print their content

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
for f in file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt; do cat $f; done
```

---

We can use wildcards to make this easier

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
for f in file?.txt; do cat $f; done
```

-   "`?`" will match any character at that position

. . .

<br>

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
for f in f*.txt; do cat $f; done
```

-   "`f*.txt`" will match any file that starts with "f" and ends with ".txt"

# You are coding!

---

Let's make a file and open it with a text editor

(I use VS Code below, but you can use any text editor)

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
touch my_bash_script.sh
code my_bash_script.sh
```

VS Code might open an authentication prompt; use your AU password

---

Add these lines to `my_bash_script.sh`

```{.bash filename="Bash script" code-line-numbers=true}
echo "Hello, World!"

for x in 1 2 3 4; do echo $x; done
```

Save and close the `my_bash_script.sh` file

---

Now, you can run `my_bash_script.sh` as a script with Bash!

```{.bash filename="Bash command line"}
bash my_bash_script.sh
```

# How to do this on your computer?

Not required! But, if you want to use a Unix-like command line on your
computer, you can!

## macOS users

You have a Terminal app already

-   Open Spotlight, type "Terminal", and press Return
-   The default shell is Zsh (not Bash), but it is *very* similar

I recommend installing Xcode command line tools

-   Open terminal and use this command:

    ```{.bash filename="Zsh command line"}
    xcode-select --install
    ```

## Windows users

You can [install Linux via the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install)

I recommend you use the default Linux distribution (Ubuntu)

Running WSL will be very similar to Red Hat (ThinLinc)
